transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, thank you for fitting me in. I... I guess I’m here because things have just completely spiraled out of control lately, and I don't really know how to fix it. It all really started when my in-laws moved into our house. We have a good-sized place, sure, but having them there, constantly in my space, it’s just... it’s been an absolute nightmare. I can’t even go into my own kitchen for a cup of coffee without an interrogation about my schedule or some passive-aggressive comment. 

And because of this constant presence, I’ve just been so incredibly keyed up all the time. I am completely worn down, right down to the bone. I mean, I’m snapping at my wife over the tiniest, most insignificant things, which I know isn't fair to her because they're her parents, but the tension in that house is just suffocating me. 

But the real wake-up call, the reason I finally made this appointment, is how it’s destroying my work. I’m a talent agent and business manager—I represent musicians, mostly—and my entire career is built on being sharp, being aggressive, and being available. But lately? I’m just sitting at my desk, staring at my phone, avoiding calls that I would normally handle immediately. I just let it ring. I can't bring myself to deal with it. And... God, just last week, I nearly let a major, and I mean major, recording contract for one of my top musicians completely fall apart. Just slip right through my fingers. I was looking at the redlines on the agreement, and I just couldn’t think straight. My brain was absolute mush. If my associate hadn't stepped in at the last possible second, the whole deal would have tanked. That is just not me. I don't drop the ball. But I just can't seem to function with this constant weight from the house dragging me down.
Have you noticed yourself losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like hobbies or time with friends?

No, no, not at all. I mean, it’s not like I don’t *want* to do things. I still very much want to see my friends and do my normal stuff. Like, I have this standing tee time on Sunday mornings with a couple of guys from the industry—a producer, another agent, guys I've known for years—and I still look forward to it all week. I really, truly do. It's my one outlet. 

It's just... well, actually getting out of the house to go do it without causing a whole scene with my mother-in-law is another story entirely. She always has some little comment queued up about how I'm "abandoning" the family on a weekend, or how nice it must be to have so much free time, which is rich considering how much I work. But the actual interest? The desire to go out and hit the links or just grab a drink at the clubhouse and talk about something other than who left a mug in the sink? That is one hundred percent still there. 

If anything, I want to escape *more* now. I just want to be around people who aren't analyzing my every move. So, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest in my hobbies or my social life. I still love reading historical biographies, I still love golfing, I still want to go out to dinner. The problem isn't that I don't care about my life outside of work and the house, it's just that the tension in the house is draining all the energy I'd normally use to actually *enjoy* those things. Because I'm still me, you know? I still like what I like. I just can't seem to catch a break long enough to actually relax and do them without feeling this massive knot in my stomach about having to go back home afterward.
Have you found yourself feeling down or hopeless about things, even outside of the stress at home?

No, no, I wouldn't say hopeless. Not at all. I mean, sure, I'm stressed. I'm incredibly stressed. The house is a pressure cooker, and it's bleeding into my work, which is terrifying, as I told you. But hopeless? Down? Like, clinically depressed? No, I don't feel like that. 

I still believe I can fix this, you know? I still believe things can get back to normal. I mean, I have to, right? I've built a really good life for myself and my wife. We have a beautiful home, I have a career that I've fought tooth and nail for, representing some truly phenomenal talent. I've negotiated deals that people said were impossible. So, I know I'm capable of handling difficult situations. I know I have the tools. 

It's just this specific situation, this relentless, daily grind of having my in-laws scrutinizing my every move, it's just throwing me off my game completely. But I don't look at my life and think, "Oh, what's the point?" or "Nothing is ever going to get better." I just think, "How do I get out from under this specific rock?" Because outside of that house, outside of that dynamic, I'm still me. I'm still driven. I still want to succeed. I still want to grow my agency. I'm not sitting around crying or feeling like the world is ending. I'm just incredibly, overwhelmingly frustrated and, frankly, exhausted by the constant friction. But hope? Yeah, I still have hope. I just need a strategy. I need a way to manage this before it completely derails the career I've spent twenty years building.
Do you find yourself constantly worrying or feeling on edge, even when you're not directly interacting with your in-laws?

No, no, I wouldn’t say that. I mean, if you’re asking if I’m just sitting around worrying about everything under the sun—like the economy, or getting sick, or just some vague sense of dread—then no, absolutely not. That’s not me. 

When I’m actually out of the house and I’m fully engaged in something else, I don’t have that constant edge. Like, if I’m at the office... well, okay, I know I said my work is suffering, and it *is*, but that’s because my brain is just so fried from the lack of peace at home, not because I’m sitting at my desk worrying about random things. When I’m away from them, if I can actually manage to focus, I feel okay. For instance, I had a lunch meeting the other day at this great spot in West Hollywood with a client’s publicist. And for that hour and a half, I was completely fine. We were talking strategy, eating, just doing the normal industry dance, and I didn't feel on edge at all. I was just me. 

But the second—and I mean the absolute second—I got back into my car and the navigation pulled up my route home, it was like a physical weight just slammed right back down onto my chest. My jaw clenched up. I immediately started running through every possible scenario of what my mother-in-law might be doing when I walk through the front door. Is she going to be in the kitchen? Is she going to make a comment about my shoes tracking in dust? Is my father-in-law going to corner me to ask about the Wi-Fi router again? 

So, the worry is highly, highly specific to them and that house. It’s not a general worry about life. If I could just magically transport them to a lovely little condo across town right this second, I swear to you, I’d be perfectly fine. I’d sleep like a baby tonight and be back to closing deals tomorrow. It’s just the sheer proximity of them that has me wound up like a top. But outside of that? No, I don't just worry for the sake of worrying.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or having a shorter temper than usual, especially in response to small things?

Oh, God, yes. Yes, absolutely. Honestly, that’s... well, that’s exactly why I’m sitting here talking to you today. Because I am just so incredibly keyed up and, frankly, completely worn down since my in-laws moved into our house. My fuse is just non-existent right now. I’m snapping at my wife over absolutely nothing—and I mean nothing. She’ll ask me a simple, innocent question about what time I'll be home, or, you know, maybe she’ll just move a stack of mail on the kitchen counter, and I just bite her head off. And she doesn't deserve that, she really doesn't, she's caught in the middle of this nightmare too, but I just have zero patience left to give. 

And the worst part is, it’s not just happening at home where I can try to apologize later. It is completely spilling over into my work. I’m avoiding calls. Important calls. Calls from managers, publicists, studio executives—calls I would normally handle immediately, you know? Usually, I just pick up the phone, charm them, negotiate, fix the problem. That's what I do. Now? I just stare at the caller ID on my desk and let it go to voicemail because I know if I pick up, I'm going to sound completely aggravated and defensive. 

It actually got so bad last week that I nearly let a major musician’s contract completely fall apart. We're talking a massive, complex deal that I've been massaging for six months, and the label's legal team sent over some minor pushback on the merchandising split. It was standard, totally normal back-and-forth stuff that I usually eat for breakfast. But I just... I couldn't think straight. My brain was so fried and I was so irritable that instead of just countering and closing the deal, I completely shut down. I ignored the email for two days. I almost blew a huge commission for my client and myself because I was too busy being silently enraged about the fact that my father-in-law had reorganized my garage the weekend before. 

So, yes, the short temper is... it's bad. It's really, really bad. I'm jeopardizing my marriage and the career I've built because I just can't seem to regulate my frustration anymore.
Have you noticed a significant loss of energy or feel unusually fatigued, even when you haven’t been doing anything particularly taxing?

No, not... well, let me clarify that, because I think it's an important distinction. Am I exhausted? Yes, absolutely, I mentioned earlier that I'm completely worn down. But it’s not some... mysterious loss of physical energy, you know? It's not like I'm just sitting in a chair, doing absolutely nothing, and suddenly I feel too weak to lift a glass of water or something. That's not it at all. 

My whole career, my entire adult life really, has been built on having a massive reserve of energy. You just don't survive in talent management if you can't run on four hours of sleep and a double espresso while juggling crises in three different time zones. I’ve always been a high-energy guy. I still am. If I go to the gym—which I still try to do, though honestly finding the mental space for it right now is a joke—I can still push through a hard workout. My body works fine. 

So, no, I don't have that kind of fatigue where I just can't physically function for no reason. If I'm feeling drained, it's because my brain is running a marathon every single second I'm in that house. Like, take this past Sunday afternoon, right? It's supposed to be my day off. I tried to just sit in the den and watch the PGA tour. Literally the least taxing thing a human being can do. Just sitting on a leather sofa. But was I relaxed? No. I was practically vibrating with tension because I could hear my mother-in-law in the kitchen loudly rearranging the Tupperware drawer—which, by the way, we had already perfectly organized. So I’m sitting there, technically doing nothing physically taxing, but my heart rate is up, my jaw is clenched tight, and I'm burning through adrenaline just trying to stop myself from walking in there and snapping at her about it. 

So by the end of the day, yeah, I’m completely wiped out. But it’s a highly, highly earned mental exhaustion from the sheer friction of my living situation, not some... biological drop in my energy levels. I’m not lethargic. I don’t feel sluggish or heavy or like I can't get out of bed. I’m just burning the candle at both ends trying to keep my sanity intact while my house is being occupied. So, no, no unusual loss of energy. Just the normal, terrible exhaustion of being under constant siege in my own living room.
Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating or making decisions, even about small things, that’s different from how you usually function?

No, no, definitely not. I don't have any issue with that at all. I mean, making decisions is literally what I get paid to do, and I do it very, very well. If you can't make a rapid-fire decision in my industry, you are going to get eaten alive. So, no, I'm not sitting around hemming and hawing over small things. I don't struggle to pick a restaurant for a client dinner, I don't freeze up when I have to decide whether to counter-offer on a back-end points deal or just walk away. My brain is completely sharp. I don't have any of that... that brain fog, or whatever people call it. 

And as for concentrating, it’s exactly the same thing. When I need to lock in, I am completely locked in. I can sit down with a fifty-page contract and spot a problematic indemnification clause in about two seconds flat. I haven't lost my edge cognitively. Not even a little bit. 

I mean, yes, like I said before, I ignored that one email for a couple of days last week, but I really need to be clear that it wasn't because I couldn't *decide* what to do, or because I couldn't concentrate on the words on the screen. I knew exactly what the counter-offer needed to be. I just... I was so consumed by how furious I was about my father-in-law messing around in my garage that I just actively chose not to engage with the work. It was a reaction born out of pure frustration, not some inability to focus my mind. 

If anything, my concentration is almost too intense right now, it’s just directed at all the wrong things. I’m hyper-focused on every little noise in my house. I can hear the exact moment my mother-in-law opens the hall closet from three rooms away, and my brain instantly zeros in on that, analyzing what she's doing. So my focus is definitely there, it's just being completely hijacked by my living situation. But as far as my actual cognitive ability to concentrate on a task or make a choice? No, that’s perfectly intact. I'm completely fine in that department.

No, not... well, let me clarify that, because I think it's an important distinction. Am I exhausted? Yes, absolutely, I mentioned earlier that I'm completely worn down. But it’s not some... mysterious loss of physical energy, you know? It's not like I'm just sitting in a chair, doing absolutely nothing, and suddenly I feel too weak to lift a glass of water or something. That's not it at all. 

My whole career, my entire adult life really, has been built on having a massive reserve of energy. You just don't survive in talent management if you can't run on four hours of sleep and a double espresso while juggling crises in three different time zones. I’ve always been a high-energy guy. I still am. If I go to the gym—which I still try to do, though honestly finding the mental space for it right now is a joke—I can still push through a hard workout. My body works fine. 

So, no, I don't have that kind of fatigue where I just can't physically function for no reason. If I'm feeling drained, it's because my brain is running a marathon every single second I'm in that house. Like, take this past Sunday afternoon, right? It's supposed to be my day off. I tried to just sit in the den and watch the PGA tour. Literally the least taxing thing a human being can do. Just sitting on a leather sofa. But was I relaxed? No. I was practically vibrating with tension because I could hear my mother-in-law in the kitchen loudly rearranging the Tupperware drawer—which, by the way, we had already perfectly organized. So I’m sitting there, technically doing nothing physically taxing, but my heart rate is up, my jaw is clenched tight, and I'm burning through adrenaline just trying to stop myself from walking in there and snapping at her about it. 

So by the end of the day, yeah, I’m completely wiped out. But it’s a highly, highly earned mental exhaustion from the sheer friction of my living situation, not some... biological drop in my energy levels. I’m not lethargic. I don’t feel sluggish or heavy or like I can't get out of bed. I’m just burning the candle at both ends trying to keep my sanity intact while my house is being occupied. So, no, no unusual loss of energy. Just the normal, terrible exhaustion of being under constant siege in my own living room.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any symptoms of depression specifically related to a diminished ability to think or concentrate, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating or making decisions, even about small things, that’s different from how you usually function?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty concentrating or making decisions, which is a specific symptom of depression or anxiety (e.g., diminished ability to think or concentrate). The patient's symptom profile does not include this as a distinct symptom, as they only have criteria for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
No, no, definitely not. I don't have any issue with that at all. I mean, making decisions is literally what I get paid to do, and I do it very, very well. If you can't make a rapid-fire decision in my industry, you are going to get eaten alive. So, no, I'm not sitting around hemming and hawing over small things. I don't struggle to pick a restaurant for a client dinner, I don't freeze up when I have to decide whether to counter-offer on a back-end points deal or just walk away. My brain is completely sharp. I don't have any of that... that brain fog, or whatever people call it. 

And as for concentrating, it’s exactly the same thing. When I need to lock in, I am completely locked in. I can sit down with a fifty-page contract and spot a problematic indemnification clause in about two seconds flat. I haven't lost my edge cognitively. Not even a little bit. 

I mean, yes, like I said before, I ignored that one email for a couple of days last week, but I really need to be clear that it wasn't because I couldn't *decide* what to do, or because I couldn't concentrate on the words on the screen. I knew exactly what the counter-offer needed to be. I just... I was so consumed by how furious I was about my father-in-law messing around in my garage that I just actively chose not to engage with the work. It was a reaction born out of pure frustration, not some inability to focus my mind. 

If anything, my concentration is almost too intense right now, it’s just directed at all the wrong things. I’m hyper-focused on every little noise in my house. I can hear the exact moment my mother-in-law opens the hall closet from three rooms away, and my brain instantly zeros in on that, analyzing what she's doing. So my focus is definitely there, it's just being completely hijacked by my living situation. But as far as my actual cognitive ability to concentrate on a task or make a choice? No, that’s perfectly intact. I'm completely fine in that department.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms are specifically tied to an identifiable stressor (in-laws moving in), with irritability, emotional exhaustion, and functional impairment in response to that stressor, without evidence of major depressive episode or generalized anxiety. The symptoms align with an adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.22). Previous candidates F43.0 (acute stress reaction) and F43.10 (post-traumatic stress disorder) are ruled out due to the chronic, situational nature of the stressor and absence of trauma or acute onset criteria.
